title: Block Gauss open chart over an arbitrary base ring
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $s\geq0$, and let $r_1,\ldots,r_s$ be positive integers. Put $E=\bigoplus_{i=1}^s A^{r_i}$, and let $\operatorname{GL}_E$ be the affine $A$-scheme whose points on a commutative $A$-algebra $B$ are the invertible matrices on $E\otimes_A B$. Its coordinate ring is the polynomial ring in the matrix entries with the determinant inverted [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Let $L,U\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_E$ be the closed subschemes of block lower and block upper unitriangular matrices, respectively: all diagonal blocks are identities and all blocks above, respectively below, the diagonal vanish. Let $D=\prod_{i=1}^s\operatorname{GL}_{r_i,A}$, embedded as block diagonal matrices. Write $\Delta_j(g)$ for the determinant of the leading block of $g$ on $\bigoplus_{i\leq j}A^{r_i}$, and let $\mathcal V\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_E$ be the principal open where $\prod_{j=1}^s\Delta_j$ is invertible. Then multiplication induces an isomorphism of $A$-schemes
$$L\times_A D\times_A U\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal V,\qquad(l,d,u)\longmapsto ldu,$$
with fibre products as in [def-pc-fibre-product]. Its inverse gives unique block Gauss factors functorially over every commutative $A$-algebra, including nonreduced algebras. The isomorphism commutes with change of the base ring and with conjugation by block diagonal invertible matrices. For $s=0$, all the displayed schemes are $\operatorname{Spec}A$ and the product of minors is $1$. The zero ring is allowed. Open and closed subschemes have the meanings of [def-weil-open-immersion, def-weil-closed-immersion].

proof.text: For $s=0$, the empty matrix has determinant $1$, there are no coordinates, and every displayed coordinate algebra is $A$. Thus all schemes and maps are the terminal $A$-scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$. Assume henceforth $s>0$. Write a lower unitriangular matrix as $I+N$. Each summand in an entry of $N^s$ requires $s+1$ strictly decreasing block indices, so $N^s=0$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}(-N)^k$ is a two-sided inverse. Therefore its strictly lower block entries are independent coordinates; the polynomial universal property and affine-spectrum correspondence represent $L$ by their polynomial ring over $A$. The upper version gives $U$ by reversing the inequalities. These presentations agree with the closed subschemes in the statement: quotienting the general matrix coordinates by the prescribed zero and identity entries leaves exactly these coordinates, and its determinant is $1$ by the permutation formula: a nonzero permutation term has row block at least column block at every position; equality of the sums of these block indices forces equality at every position, and the identity diagonal blocks then force the identity permutation. For each block, $A[d_{i,ab},\det(d_i)^{-1}]$ represents invertible matrices: a matrix inverse makes its determinant a unit by multiplicativity, and a unit determinant gives the inverse $\det(d_i)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(d_i)$ by the adjugate identity. These are the coordinate presentations of the factors of $D$.

proof.text: By the affine fibre-product statement, $X=L\times_A D\times_A U$ is affine, and its ring $C$ is the tensor product over $A$ of the coordinate rings of all factors. The tensor-product universal property identifies maps $C\to B$ with independent choices of all these factor coordinates in any commutative $A$-algebra $B$. Combining this with polynomial evaluation and localization, $C$ is the polynomial ring on the lower, diagonal and upper block entries with the diagonal-block determinants inverted. Put $H=A[g_{ab},\det(g)^{-1}]$ and $f=\prod_{j=1}^s\Delta_j$. Clause (b) of the affine-open localization statement gives $\mathcal V=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $R=H_f$ (Stacks 01I3, schemes-lemma-standard-open-affine). The localization universal property (Stacks 00CP, algebra-proposition-universal-property-localization) identifies $\mathcal V(B)$ with invertible matrices for which $f(g)$ is a unit. This means every $\Delta_j(g)$ is a unit: if $fv=1$, then $v\prod_{k\ne j}\Delta_k$ is its inverse; conversely multiply the individual inverses. No reducedness or nonzero-ring assumption enters.

proof.text: For a triple $(l,d,u)$ over any commutative $A$-algebra $B$, its product restricted to the first $j$ blocks is $l_{\le j}d_{\le j}u_{\le j}$. Indeed the intermediate block index in $l_{ik}d_ku_{kh}$ must satisfy $k\le i$ and $k\le h$, so $i,h\le j$ forces $k\le j$. Repeatedly split off the first block and use the Schur determinant identity with pivot $I$: every lower or upper unitriangular leading matrix has determinant $1$. Applied with zero off-diagonal blocks and invertible diagonal pivots, the same identity gives $\det(d_{\le j})=\prod_{i\le j}\det(d_i)$. Multiplicativity now gives $\Delta_j(ldu)=\prod_{i\le j}\det(d_i)$, a unit. Here every nonempty leading size is at least $1$, as required by the determinant-multiplicativity node. Matrix multiplication is polynomial. Apply it to the universal triple over $C$; the just-proved units allow evaluation $H_f\to C$ by localization. The affine-spectrum correspondence gives the desired multiplication morphism $m:X\to\mathcal V$.

proof.text:
Induct on the number of blocks, uniformly for every commutative $A$-algebra $B$, to prove existence of factors for $g\in\mathcal V(B)$. The empty case is step 1; for one block take $(I,g,I)$. For $s\ge2$, split off the first block and write $g=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}P&Q\\ T&W\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Since $\det P=\Delta_1(g)$ is a unit, the adjugate identity gives $P^{-1}=(\det P)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(P)$. Put $S=W-TP^{-1}Q$. For $1\le k\le s-1$, apply the Schur determinant identity to the first $k+1$ blocks of $g$ to obtain $\Delta_{k+1}(g)=\det(P)\Delta_k(S)$. Hence all $\Delta_k(S)$ are units, and the full one makes $S$ invertible by the adjugate identity. Induction gives $S=l'd'u'$. Set $L_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\ TP^{-1}&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $U_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&P^{-1}Q\\ 0&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The Schur factorization yields
$$g=\bigl(L_0\operatorname{diag}(I,l')\bigr)\operatorname{diag}(P,d')\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(I,u')U_0\bigr).$$
The first factor is lower unitriangular, the middle is block diagonal with invertible blocks, and the last is upper unitriangular. This completes the induction over arbitrary $B$.

proof.text:
For uniqueness use induction on the same block count. Empty and one-block factorizations are forced. Write any factorization as
$$l=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\ x&l'\end{pmatrix},\quad d=\operatorname{diag}(p,d'),\quad u=\begin{pmatrix}I&y\\ 0&u'\end{pmatrix}.$$
Comparing its product with $g=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}P&Q\\ T&W\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ gives $P=p$, $Q=py$, $T=xp$, and $W=xpy+l'd'u'$. Thus $p=P$, $y=P^{-1}Q$, $x=TP^{-1}$ and $l'd'u'=W-TP^{-1}Q=S$. Inductive uniqueness on $S$ determines all remaining blocks. A homomorphism of $A$-algebras preserves products, identities and inverses; applying it to factors therefore gives the unique factors of the image matrix. This proves functoriality, including maps to the zero algebra.

source.place: Agent-written arbitrary-base matrix argument supporting §23h, (152)–(153), Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510–511; uniqueness by comparing four blocks, and naturality by uniqueness.

proof.text: Apply step 4 to the universal matrix $g_R$ over $R=H_f$. The resulting matrices $l_R,d_R,u_R$ have entries in $R$ and invertible diagonal blocks. Polynomial evaluation and localization give a unique map $C\to R$ taking the universal factor coordinates to these entries and each inverted determinant to its inverse. This defines an $A$-morphism $v:\mathcal V\to X$ by the affine-spectrum correspondence. Existence gives $l_Rd_Ru_R=g_R$, so $m\circ v$ is the identity on the entry coordinates of $H$ and hence on $H_f$ by localization uniqueness. Conversely apply step 5 over $C$ to the universal triple: the factors of its product computed by $v$ must be the original triple. Thus $v\circ m$ fixes every entry coordinate in every factor and each inverse determinant; polynomial, localization and tensor-product uniqueness give the identity on $C$. The affine-spectrum correspondence now proves that $m$ and $v$ are inverse scheme isomorphisms. Evaluation under $R\to B$ agrees with the unique pointwise factors by step 5. In particular the argument tests universal rings, not merely field-valued points.

proof.text: For a ring map $A\to A'$, base change of any displayed affine coordinate algebra $K$ is $A'\otimes_A K$ by the affine fibre-product statement. Its maps to a commutative $A'$-algebra $B$ are exactly $A$-algebra maps $K\to B$ by the tensor universal property. For polynomial and localized polynomial $K$ these are exactly the choices of the same entry coordinates in $B$ with the same determinant units, by evaluation and localization. These universal properties give the canonical identification with the coordinate algebra defined directly over $A'$: the two maps sending every entry and inverse determinant to its namesake compose to identities by the same uniqueness properties. This identifies the base changes of $L,D,U,\mathcal V$ with their $A'$ versions. Under these identifications multiplication sends each matrix entry to the same sum of products, so its base change is the multiplication constructed over $A'$. The base-changed inverse is the inverse of that multiplication, hence equals the inverse over $A'$ by uniqueness of an inverse. This proves the claimed compatibility for every ring map, including nonflat maps and maps to the zero ring.

proof.text: Let $h=\operatorname{diag}(h_i)$ be block diagonal invertible over $B$. Conjugation sends block $(i,j)$ to $h_i g_{ij}h_j^{-1}$, so it preserves zero blocks, identity blocks and invertibility of diagonal blocks. For the first $j$ blocks put $h_{\le j}=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_j)$. Their leading matrix is conjugated by $h_{\le j}$, so determinant multiplicativity gives $\Delta_j(hgh^{-1})=\Delta_j(g)$, using $\det(h_{\le j})\det(h_{\le j}^{-1})=1$. Thus conjugation preserves $\mathcal V$. Associativity gives $(hlh^{-1})(hdh^{-1})(huh^{-1})=h(ldu)h^{-1}$, and step 5 gives equivariance of the inverse. These are scheme identities: the products $D\times_A X$ and $D\times_A\mathcal V$ are affine by the affine-product node; use their universal matrices in the calculation. Entries of $h_i^{-1}$ are regular there by the adjugate formula and the inverted diagonal determinants. Consequently the formulas define the action morphisms by polynomial evaluation and localization; the equalities on universal entries imply equal coordinate-ring maps and hence equal scheme morphisms. This proves conjugation equivariance over $A$ and after arbitrary base change. The $s=0$ case was already settled in step 1.
